notes.meaning: God gave Jeremiah a new message to preach to the nation. Many teachers believe this took place near the beginning of King Jehoiakim's reign, when Judah quickly turned back to idols after good King Josiah had died.

Jeremiah was told to stand right at the entrance of the Lord's temple. From that spot he could speak to huge crowds coming from all over Judah for a religious feast. Even people who show up to worship still need to hear God's truth about their sins.
The Lord told the worshippers to change their daily habits and turn from evil. If they truly corrected their ways, God promised He would allow them to keep living peacefully in their homeland.

The people chanted a popular slogan about the temple, believing God would never let His holy building be harmed. Jeremiah warned them that trusting in empty words like this was a lie. A sacred building cannot protect people who refuse to obey God.

God explained what real repentance looks like in everyday life. They had to treat one another fairly, stop mistreating the foreigner, orphan, and widow, stop murdering the innocent, and quit serving false gods. If they showed this kind of genuine justice, God would let them dwell in the land He had promised to their ancestors.
Jeremiah pointed out that the people were trusting in completely useless lies. Chanting slogans about the temple would bring them zero profit or protection when God's judgment arrived.

The people constantly broke God's commandments by stealing, murdering, committing adultery, lying under oath, and worshipping Baal and strange gods. Yet they still walked into God's temple and claimed they were safe, as if their worship gave them permission to keep sinning. Acting like this treated God as if He approved of their evil crimes.

The Lord asked if the people thought His holy house was a hideout for criminals, like a cave where robbers take cover between crimes. God warned that He had seen right through their phony religion. Jesus later quoted these words when He drove the dishonest merchants out of the temple courts.

God told the crowd to look back at Shiloh, the town where Israel's tabernacle had stood for hundreds of years. Because the priests and people there fell into gross wickedness, God abandoned that sanctuary and let it be ruined. A place's past holiness will never shield it from judgment if the people defile it.

The Lord had reached out to Judah with deep care and urgency, speaking to them again and again through His prophets, but they refused to listen. Because of this stubborn disobedience, God promised to destroy the temple in Jerusalem just as He had destroyed Shiloh.

God warned that He would drive Judah out of His sight and into exile. The northern ten tribes, represented by Ephraim, had already been conquered and carried off for their idolatry, and Judah was about to suffer the very same fate.
God told Jeremiah not to intercede or pray for this people anymore. Their hearts had become so hardened and their rebellion was so complete that God's decree of judgment was now final.

The Lord told the prophet to look around at what was happening in the streets of Jerusalem and the towns of Judah. Their false worship was not done in secret; it was practiced boldly in broad daylight.

Whole families joined together in idolatry: children picked up firewood, fathers lit the flames, and mothers kneaded dough to bake sacrificial cakes for a goddess called the Queen of Heaven. They also poured out drink offerings to other gods, deliberately provoking the Lord.

differ.view: Some evangelicals connect the title 'Queen of Heaven' here to the traditional Catholic title for Mary, warning that devotion and prayers directed to her carry echoes of ancient idolatry.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching explains that Jeremiah was condemning an ancient pagan goddess, which has no connection to honoring Jesus' mother centuries later, and notes that Catholics offer worship and sacrifice to God alone.

notes.meaning: The Lord asked whether their rebellion really injured Him. Human sin cannot harm the Almighty; instead, their wicked deeds harmed only themselves, bringing shame and ruin on their own faces.

God announced that His fierce anger would pour out like an unquenchable fire on the entire land. This judgment would strike not only the people, but also their farm animals, trees, and crops. Sin damages the physical world as well as human lives.

God spoke with sharp irony, telling the people to go ahead and eat their burnt offerings. Burnt offerings were supposed to be given completely to God on the altar, but the Lord rejected their empty rituals so thoroughly that they might as well treat the holy meat as common food.

When God brought Israel out of Egypt, His central command was not about animal sacrifices, but about wholehearted obedience to His voice. He promised that if they walked in His ways, He would be their God and they would be His people. Religious ceremonies have no value to God if people refuse to live by His moral law.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars read these verses as evidence that Israel offered no sacrifices in the wilderness, or that the laws of sacrifice in the Pentateuch were created much later in Israel's history.

notes.meaning: Israel refused to listen or pay attention to God's instruction. Instead, they stubbornly followed their own evil desires, turning their backs on Him and going backward into worse sin rather than forward into holiness.

From the day Israel left Egypt until Jeremiah's time, God continuously sent prophets to guide the nation and call them to repent. Yet the people refused to listen, hardened their hearts, and ended up acting more corruptly than their ancestors had.
God warned Jeremiah in advance that the people would not listen when he delivered this message. Even though they would ignore his call, the prophet still had to preach the truth faithfully.
Jeremiah was told to announce God's final verdict against the nation. They were a people who refused to obey the Lord or accept any correction, and truth had completely vanished from their mouths.

Jerusalem was called to cut off her hair and mourn on the bare hills like a grieving mother. In Israel, shaving the hair showed deep sorrow, and here it also showed that the city had lost its special dedication to the Lord. God had rejected this generation because of the wrath they had brought upon themselves.
The people of Judah committed an outrageous sin right under God's eye. They set up disgusting pagan idols inside the Lord's own temple, polluting the very building that bore His holy name.

The people built pagan altars at Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom, just outside the city, where they burned their own sons and daughters in sacrifice to Moloch. God declared that this horrifying cruelty was something He had never commanded, desired, or intended in any way.

differ.view: Some evangelicals teach that the phrase 'nor did it enter My mind' indicates God does not have advance knowledge of every future free human choice, while most evangelicals hold that God knows all things and that this phrase simply means child sacrifice was completely contrary to His will.

notes.meaning: God warned that the valley would soon be renamed the Valley of Slaughter. So many people would be killed during the coming invasion that the valley would be filled with graves until there was no room left to bury the dead.
The bodies of the dead would lie exposed on the ground as food for scavenging birds and wild beasts. There would be no one left with the strength or will to frighten the animals away.

The Lord promised to silence all sounds of celebration, joy, and wedding music across Jerusalem and the towns of Judah. War and exile would sweep through the land, turning the once-thriving nation into an empty wasteland.
